items.definition: The false feeling of understanding a topic that comes from easy access to answers rather than from real comprehension.
The pattern in which people with little skill in a domain overestimate their ability, because the skill needed to judge answers is the same skill needed to give them.
The tendency to seek out, remember and trust information that supports existing beliefs while discounting the rest.
The tendency to forget information that is easy to find online, while remembering how to find it.
The habit of holding your own beliefs with the right amount of confidence: strong when the evidence is strong, weak when it is weak.
The skill of finding, judging and using information: telling a primary source from an opinion, and evidence from an anecdote.
The false feeling of competence that comes from producing results with powerful tools rather than from owned ability.
Results and confidence produced by tools, which the user experiences as personal ability.
The systematic tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one's own knowledge and the odds of one's success.
The tendency to trust automated systems more than one's own judgment, especially under pressure or fatigue.
The accuracy of your self-assessment: how closely your confidence matches your actual performance.
The weakening of a skill through long disuse, often because a tool has performed it instead.
The state in which incoming information exceeds the capacity to process it, so each new item reduces the value of the ones before it.
The total amount of mental effort being used by working memory at one time.
The market in which businesses compete for people's limited attention and resell it to advertisers.
The proportion of useful information (signal) to everything else (noise) in a stream of content.
Familiarity with the surface of many topics without understanding of how any of them works.
The ability you have to do something, whatever you decide to do it for.
items.example: He had the capacity to read a face well, and the capacity was never the question.

items.definition: The aim that is behind an act: what the act is for.
items.example: The motive was to keep the machine running, and the motive decided the rest.

items.definition: The way an aim is carried out: the tools, the words and the methods used.
items.example: The means were ordinary tools used in an ordinary way.

items.definition: An act repeated until it can be done without thinking about it.
items.example: It was a habit, and the habit had been built one small repetition at a time.

items.definition: What a person does as a rule, when nobody is checking.
items.example: Character is what you do when nobody is checking.

items.definition: The short space in which one argument is weighed against another.
items.example: Deliberation took two minutes, and the two minutes were enough.

items.definition: The argument made against a decision that is still being considered.
items.example: The counter-argument was short, and it changed the decision.

items.definition: A sudden push to act before you have thought it through.
items.example: The impulse to reply at once was stronger than the answer.

items.definition: The pull of a gain that somebody else pays the cost of.
items.example: The temptation was the extra 200 $ that the supplier would pay for.

items.definition: The people who are present and watching when you act.
items.example: With the customer in the room, the audience changed what he said.

items.definition: Holding a decision back for a short time so that the second argument can be made.
items.example: A little self-control before the reply is cheaper than a retraction later.

items.definition: The sense that tells you an act would hurt somebody.
items.example: His conscience told him the report would hurt the supplier.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: A rule that a group follows although nobody has written it down.
items.example: The unwritten rule was that nobody questioned the schedule.

items.definition: A measurable stand-in for something you cannot see directly, such as a score standing in for ability.
items.example: The score is only a proxy; the ability itself is what the employer needs.

items.definition: A fact that supports a claim, so that the claim does not rest on opinion alone.
items.example: The temperature log is evidence that the pump ran hot.

items.definition: The capacity to do a task well, in a real situation, under real conditions.
items.example: The ability to find the fault was there; the procedure had never been written down.

items.definition: The quality of a test that asks whether it measures what it claims to measure.
items.example: The test was reliable but not valid for the work we do.

items.definition: The quality of a measurement that gives a similar result when it is repeated.
items.example: Two markers gave the same result, so the marking was reliable.

items.definition: The ability to use what you learned in one situation in a different situation.
items.example: The training transferred well: the same method worked on a new line.

items.definition: The rise in a test result that comes from having seen the material before.
items.example: The second attempt scored higher, and the practice effect explains much of it.

items.definition: The usual result of a group, used as the point of comparison.
items.example: Compare the mark with the norm for that group, not with the mark alone.

items.definition: The power of a test to separate the people who know the material from those who do not.
items.example: A test that everybody passes has poor discriminability.
